disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), Combined Presentation, is characterized by a persistent pattern of both inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity that is inconsistent with developmental level, present in at least two settings, and associated with clinically significant functional impairment. In adults and older adults, it often presents as chronic disorganization, difficulty sustaining effort, inner restlessness, and impulsive decision-making more than overt disruptive behavior, and symptoms typically have been present since childhood even if they were never formally diagnosed. The course is usually chronic, with symptom expression and impact shifting across the lifespan in response to environmental demands, compensatory strategies, and comorbidities. It is distinguished from anxiety, mood, and personality disorders by the early onset, pervasive cognitive and behavioral regulation difficulties, and a characteristic response to structured supports and stimulant or non-stimulant pharmacotherapy.

narrative.personality: She is pragmatic, detail-focused about her work, and intellectually competitive in quiet hobbies like puzzles and chess, with a strong sense of responsibility toward others she mentors.
narrative.stressor: After her divorce and semi-retirement from a higher-responsibility facilities manager role, Syble took on multiple part-time cleaning contracts while informally trying to launch a small consulting service on green cleaning practices. The shift from a single, structured job to juggling several sites, irregular hours, and self-directed business tasks exposed long-standing difficulties in planning, prioritizing, and pacing herself that she had previously managed through rigid routines and checklists. Over the next year and a half, she found herself overbooking walkthroughs, double-committing to meetings with property owners, and talking over potential clients and junior staff during discussions because she felt pressured to “get everything out” before she lost track, which strained professional relationships and undermined her confidence as a mentor. When a key contract renewal was jeopardized after a contentious meeting where she repeatedly cut off the building supervisor and missed several agreed follow-ups, she became worried that something beyond normal stress or aging was interfering with her work and sought psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My coworkers and clients keep telling me I cut them off and butt into conversations before they can finish their thoughts.”

narrative.personality: She is methodical and conscientious, with a strong preference for structure and planning, yet she is also driven and constantly engaged in work and mentally stimulating hobbies.
narrative.stressor: About two years ago, Natalie was promoted to lead a cross-functional aerospace project that significantly increased her responsibility for timelines, regulatory coordination, and team communication. The role demanded long stretches of focused planning, frequent context-switching between meetings and design work, and sustained attention to detail under tight, evolving deadlines, which amplified underlying organizational and self-regulation vulnerabilities she had previously contained with meticulous personal systems. As the project intensified, she found herself unable to slow down or mentally disengage, filling every spare moment with work or complex hobbies, pacing through the office, and taking on additional tasks rather than delegating, which paradoxically led to missed milestones, friction with colleagues, and exhaustion at home despite her efforts to appear composed. After her manager raised concerns about her erratic work patterns and her spouse noted that she “never sits still” and seems unable to relax even in the evenings, Natalie worried that her constant drive and difficulty modulating her activity were not just normal ambition, prompting her to seek a psychiatric assessment.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I’m constantly on the go and can’t ever just sit still or switch off, even when I really want to.”

narrative.personality: He is a routine-oriented, quietly generous retiree who enjoys solitary, hands-on projects and teaching practical skills to others in a calm, steady manner.
narrative.stressor: When Lazaro retired a little over two years ago, he lost the external structure and clear deadlines that his years as a craftsman had provided, and he tried to fill the time with gardening, woodworking, and volunteering at the senior center. Without the built-in rhythm of a workday, he began starting multiple leisure projects at once—carving, recipe writing, music listening—finding it surprisingly hard to settle into any of them quietly for more than brief periods, which contrasted with the patience he remembered having on the job. Over the following year and ten months, this restlessness began to intrude on his enjoyment of activities he values, such as interrupting his own woodworking to repeatedly get up, change music, or check on the garden, and making it difficult to sit through calm family gatherings or focused mentoring sessions without repeatedly shifting gears. When his wife and adult children gently commented that he seemed unable to simply sit and enjoy his hobbies or conversations without constantly breaking the flow, and he noticed frustration in his grandchildren during shared projects, he agreed to consult a psychiatrist to understand whether there was an underlying attention problem contributing to these changes.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t seem to just sit and enjoy my hobbies quietly anymore—I’m always getting up and breaking the flow.”
